HR@10 against 99 fixed negatives measures success within that 100-item candidate set; it does not establish full-catalog ranking quality. Sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation ([Krichene & Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). A single-negative score margin diagnoses one pairwise comparison, not whether the positive outranks enough of the 99 candidates to enter the top ten. For this benchmark, retain the pinned evaluator and supplement margins with measured positive ranks, top-ten boundary margins, and per-user hit indicators; these are diagnostic recommendations, not alternative selection metrics.

For comparing two models, a suitable adaptation of [paired bootstrap resampling](https://aclanthology.org/W04-3250/) is to resample the 200 users with replacement separately within each category, using identical sampled user indices for both models. Recompute each category’s mean hit difference, then average the four differences with equal weight. Report the observed macro difference and a bootstrap confidence interval. Assuming independent users within categories, this estimates user-sampling uncertainty conditional on these four datasets, fixed candidates, and fitted models; it excludes training-seed, candidate-resampling, and new-domain uncertainty.

Repeated hyperparameter trials can overfit validation noise: selecting the largest observed score creates optimistic performance estimates ([Cawley & Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)). A fixed GPU budget limits search but does not remove selection bias. Record every trial, validation query, and consumed GPU-second, including failures; predefine stopping and selection rules. Treat winner-versus-baseline validation intervals as exploratory because ordinary paired bootstrapping does not correct adaptive selection. Leave final generalization assessment to the host’s untouched held-out evaluation.
